title: Emergent spatial structure in the gut microbiota is driven by bacterial growth and gut contractions
experiments_summary:
1. MACROSCOPIC SPATIAL DISTRIBUTION: Gnotobiotic mice (3MM: B. thetaiotaomicron, E. rectale, E. coli) were used; cecum tip and base sections were fixed, cryosectioned (5 µm), stained via fluorescent in-situ hybridization (FISH), and imaged by confocal microscopy. Bacterial coordinates were determined by custom Matlab image analysis. OligoMM12 and SPF mice underwent the same spatial sampling with 16S rRNA sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq 6000, DADA2 pipeline) to assess compositional differences between cecum regions; Jensen-Shannon divergences were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests.

2. PARTICLE FLOW TRACKING: SPF mice received three sequential oral gavages of differently colored 1-µm fluorescent microspheres 40 min apart; ceca were harvested 5 h post-first gavage, sectioned, and imaged to track spatiotemporal bead distribution between base, tip epithelium, and tip center.

3. MICROSCALE BACTERIAL CLUSTERING: Bacterial spatial distribution in 3MM cecum sections was quantified using the inhomogeneous Ripley's H(r) function (spatstat R package), with Studentized permutation tests (1,000 permutations) to assess significance. Clustering was compared between cecum tip and base, and between epithelial and center regions.

4. ABIOTIC PARTICLE CLUSTERING CONTROL: 3MM mice were gavaged with 10^9 1-µm fluorescent beads; cecum was harvested 4.5 h later, sectioned, and bead clustering analyzed with the same H(r) method to distinguish biotic from abiotic contributions to clustering.

5. ROLE OF SIGA: IgA responses against 3MM species were measured by flow cytometry in intestinal lavages from ex-germ-free mice colonized for 4 weeks vs. mice bred with 3MM from birth. E. coli clustering (H function) was compared between these groups using Studentized permutation tests.

6. ROLE OF CHEMOTAXIS AND FLAGELLA: Germ-free mice were monocolonized with mCherry-labeled wild-type E. coli Z1331, a chemotaxis mutant (cheY::aphT), or a flagella mutant (flhD::aphT). After 3 days, ceca were collected, sectioned, and bacterial clustering quantified by H(r) analysis.

7. ROLE OF NICHE SIZE: mCherry-labeled B. theta was introduced into OligoMM12 mice (smaller niche) and 3MM mice (larger niche); after 3 days colonization, bacterial counts and H(r)-based clustering were compared between groups.

8. RHEOLOGY OF GUT CONTENT: Fresh cecum content from 3MM mice and ileal effluent from 4 human ileostomy volunteers (NBMISI study) were analyzed using a stress-controlled parallel-plate rheometer (Anton Paar MCR302, 25 mm plates, 0.8 mm gap, 37°C, sandpaper to minimize wall slip). Oscillatory strain amplitude sweeps (γ = 0.1–1000%, ω = 1 rad/s) and frequency sweeps (γ = 0.1%, ω = 0.1–100 rad/s) measured storage (G') and loss (G'') moduli. Creep tests (10–50 Pa, 300 s each) on three independent mouse cecum samples estimated yield stress. Digesta density was measured gravimetrically.

9. STOKES SECOND PROBLEM MODELING: Rheological parameters were combined with a Stokes Second Problem fluid dynamics model of oscillating gut wall contractions to estimate the depth from the gut wall at which shear stress exceeds the yield limit, using measured values for digesta viscosity, density, contraction amplitude, and frequency.

10. PHARMACOLOGICAL MANIPULATION OF GUT CONTRACTIONS: 3MM mice received intraperitoneal injections of ricinoleic acid (8 mg in 100 µl PBS, to increase contractions), loperamide (0.4 mg in 100 µl PBS, to decrease contractions), or PBS control. Mice were euthanized at 1.5 h (all drugs) or 6 h (loperamide, two-dose protocol). Cecum sections were FISH-stained and bacterial clustering assessed by H(r) analysis with Studentized permutation tests.
